objective: Determine the distance of a star from its parallax, a Cepheid period, the distance modulus or Hubble's law, convert between AU, light years and parsecs, and relate apparent magnitude, absolute magnitude and luminosity.
Relate the luminosity of a star to its radius and surface temperature with L = 4πR²σT⁴, place it in the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, and estimate its mass, energy output and lifetime with L ∝ M^3.5.
Calculate the mean density, the Schwarzschild radius R = 2GM/c² and the limits of rotation of compact objects such as white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes.
Apply Newton's law of gravitation to astronomical systems: the period of a binary star, the field of a spherical mass from Gauss's law, and the Jeans criterion for the collapse of a gas cloud.
Relate charge, current, time and energy with ΔQ = I·Δt and W = Q·ΔV, including battery capacities in mAh, and tell the conventional current from the motion of electrons and ions.
Calculate electric power and energy with P = ΔV·I = R·I² = ΔV²/R from device ratings, and predict by ratios how the power changes when voltage, current or resistance change.
Find the source voltage, internal resistance and terminal voltage of cells combined in series and in parallel.
Calculate the reactances ωL and 1/(ωC), the impedance Z = V0/I0 and the phase shift of series and parallel RLC circuits with phasors, and read the phase shift from a time shift.
Use the exponential decay I(t) = I0·e^(−t/τ) with τ = L/R to find the current or the time after an RL circuit is switched off.

Describe an AC voltage by its amplitude, rms value, frequency and period, derive rms values by integration, and explain with the transformer ratio why transmitting power at high voltage reduces losses.
Relate apparent power, effective power, power factor and phase shift in an AC circuit with P = V_rms·I_rms·cos Δφ.
Calculate the resistance of a wire from R = ρ·L/A and solve it for the length, the cross-section or the resistivity.
Calculate the change of resistance with temperature from R = R0·(1 + α·Δϑ), and use it to explain the non-linear I–V characteristic of a light bulb and to find its operating point.
Calculate the drift velocity of the electrons in a wire from I = n·A·e·v and explain why it is so small.
Calculate the capacitance from C = Q/ΔV and from C = ε0·εr·A/d, relate the field to the charge with E = Q/(ε0·A), and predict how plate area, gap or dielectric change C and E.
Calculate the energy stored in a capacitor, W = ½·C·ΔV², and the energy density of an electric field, w = ½·ε0·E², and relate them to other forms of energy.

Relate an amount of charge to the number of elementary charges, Q = N·e, find the charges of identical conductors after contact from charge conservation, and explain charging by contact and by influence.

Calculate the force between two point charges with Coulomb's law and the field E = k·Q/r² of a point charge or charged sphere, solve for a charge or distance, and compare the electric with the gravitational force.
Add the electric fields of point charges and uniform fields component-wise and find the point where the net field vanishes.

Use W = q·ΔV and the Coulomb potential energy E = k·q1·q2/r with energy conservation to find speeds, energies in electronvolts and distances of closest approach, and compare electric with gravitational potential.
Derive the electric field or force of a continuous charge distribution, such as a ring, an arc, a wire or a plate, by integrating the contributions of its charge elements.
Apply Gauss's law with a symmetric Gaussian surface to find the electric flux or the field of a spherical, cylindrical or planar charge distribution.
Find the potential difference of a charge distribution by integrating its field, and the field as the negative gradient of the potential, E = −∇V.
Calculate the capacitance of cylindrical and spherical capacitors from their geometry and show that for small gaps they approach the parallel plate capacitor.
Derive the field of an electric dipole with its far-field approximation and the net force on a dipole in a non-uniform field.
Calculate the motional emf ε = v·B·L of a conductor moving across a magnetic field, and show that the electrical power it delivers equals the mechanical power needed to move it.
Apply Faraday's law to rotating conductors and coils, with the generator amplitude ε0 = N·A·B·ω, and to the ideal transformer, and express the magnetic flux and its unit through B and the area.
Calculate the size of the magnetic force F = q·v·B·sin θ on a moving charge, or the field from the force, and describe the path of a charge in combined electric and magnetic fields.

Calculate the self-induced emf ε = −L·ΔI/Δt and the inductance of a solenoid, the energy W = ½·L·I² stored in a coil and the magnetic energy density B²/(2μ0), also in the energy balance of an LC circuit.

Calculate the magnetic field of a long straight wire from B = μ0·I/(2πr), superpose it with the fields of other wires and with the Earth's field, resolved into horizontal and vertical components with the inclination.
Calculate the magnetic field of a circular loop or short coil on its axis, and of a Helmholtz coil as the superposition of two coaxial loops.
Calculate the field inside a solenoid from B = μ0·μr·N·I/L, solve it for N, I or μr, and describe how para- and diamagnetic materials change the field.
Classify a differential equation as linear or nonlinear and time-invariant or not, and convert a higher-order linear ODE into a first-order system with its coefficient matrix, and back.
Calculate the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix and build the solution of a linear system as a superposition of eigenvector solutions fitted to the initial conditions.
Classify the fixed point of a 2D linear system as node, saddle, centre or spiral from its trace, determinant or eigenvalues, and sketch its phase portrait.

Model coupled processes such as decay chains, reactions, populations and the damped oscillator as linear systems, and relate their eigenvalues to the behaviour, such as under-, over- and critical damping.
Integrate a spherically symmetric function in spherical coordinates and evaluate the radial integrals that arise.
Compute vector products from components and interpret their direction, and express sine and cosine through complex exponentials with Euler's formula.
Give a measured result with its absolute and relative uncertainty and propagate uncertainties through products, powers and functions, also with the min/max method.
Convert energies and masses between joules, kilograms, electronvolts and eV/c².

Relate power, energy, time and efficiency with P = E/Δt and η = E_out/E_in, and apply the related laws of momentum conservation in a perfectly inelastic collision and of hydrostatic pressure p = ρ·g·h.
Calculate time, distance or speed of a uniform motion from v = Δs/Δt with unit conversions, and read an acceleration with its sign as the slope of the v(t) graph.
Calculate nuclear binding energies and the energy released in decays and reactions from the mass defect with ΔE = Δm·c², also with the liquid-drop formula.
Describe α, β and γ radiation, write their decay equations, and apply the decay law with half-life and activity.
Calculate absorbed, equivalent and effective doses from energy, mass, dose rate and weighting factors, the shielding by I = I0·e^(−μd), and assess the health risk.
Calculate the minima of a single slit, b·sin α = k·λ, and of a circular aperture, and use them to find the size of a slit or an obstacle.

Find the thickness of a thin film from the condition for constructive or destructive interference with the phase jumps on reflection, relate fringe shifts in a Michelson interferometer to the mirror displacement, and explain why interference needs coherent light.
Determine the position, size and type of an image with the thin lens equation 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i, also for a system of two lenses.
Sketch the path of a ray through a glass body with refraction and total internal reflection, and calculate the reflected fraction of the intensity at an interface.
Superpose two harmonic oscillations: find the resulting amplitude for equal frequencies from the phase shift, and the beat frequency for slightly different frequencies.

Calculate the period of a mass–spring oscillator from T = 2π·√(m/k), also hanging vertically where gravity only shifts the equilibrium, and of a physical or torsional pendulum from its moment of inertia.
Use energy conservation in a mechanical oscillator and in an LC circuit, ½CV² + ½LI² = const., to relate displacement, speed and amplitude, and calculate the frequency f = 1/(2π·√(LC)).

Characterise a damped or driven oscillator by its damping coefficient δ, the damping ratio ζ = δ/ω0 (weak, critical, strong) and the Q factor of its resonance curve, and show that a given function solves its differential equation.

Determine the period and the linear or exponential envelope of a damped oscillation from measured data, and relate the envelope to the damping coefficient, the half-life and the remaining energy (E ∝ A²).
Set up the equations of motion of coupled oscillators and find their normal-mode frequencies and mode shapes.
Derive the phase and group velocity of a de Broglie wave and show that the stationary states of the infinite well are orthonormal.
Determine the number of orbitals in a shell or subshell and the orbital angular momentum L = ħ·√(ℓ(ℓ+1)) from the quantum numbers n and ℓ.

Evaluate the Bohr radius and the ground-state energy from fundamental constants, calculate the levels E_n = E_1/n² and the energies of transitions and ionisation, and scale them to hydrogen-like and exotic atoms.
Describe the X-ray tube and its spectrum: the heat produced, the characteristic lines from Moseley's law, the maximum of the bremsstrahlung, and the attenuation in matter.
Calculate the momentum p = γ·m·v, the energy E = γ·m·c² and the kinetic energy (γ − 1)·m·c² of a particle, use E² = (pc)² + (mc²)², and compare with the classical expressions.
Relate a change of energy to a change of mass with ΔE = Δm·c², and find the energy for pair production, annihilation and the threshold of particle production in collisions.
Derive relations of special relativity from the definitions, such as identities of the Lorentz factor, the energy–momentum relation, massless particles and the relativistic form of F = dp/dt.
Calculate the Lorentz factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) and use it for time dilation and length contraction, also with γ ≈ 1 + v²/(2c²) for small speeds and for lengths perpendicular to the motion.
Combine velocities with u = (v + u′)/(1 + v·u′/c²) and show that it keeps the speed of light invariant and reduces to the Galilean rule at low speeds.
Apply the relativistic Doppler factor √((1+β)/(1−β)) to find a shifted wavelength or the speed of a source.
Apply the ideal gas law pV = nRT with absolute temperatures to find the pressure, temperature or particle density of a gas.
Set up heat balances with Q = c·m·Δθ to find a mixing temperature or a mass, use the heating value and efficiency of a heat engine, and the water content of air from the relative humidity.
Relate the temperature of a black body to its peak wavelength with Wien's law and to its radiated power with the Stefan–Boltzmann law, also in an energy balance.
Relate the wavelength and the frequency of electromagnetic waves with c = λ·f.
Relate the intensity of an electromagnetic wave to its power, area, distance (inverse square law), field amplitude (I ∝ E²) and energy, and verify that a plane wave satisfies Maxwell's equations.
Relate wavelength, frequency, period, wave number and speed with v = λ·f, and read or construct the wave function y(x,t) of a travelling wave.
Calculate the speed of sound in a gas, liquid or solid from its material properties and use it for the standing waves in a rod.
Convert between sound intensity, pressure amplitude and sound intensity level L = 10·log(I/I0), add the intensities of several sources, and read the loudness in phon.
Combine musical intervals by multiplying their frequency ratios, express them in octaves, semitones and cents, and compare just with equally tempered intervals.
Calculate the frequency heard when the source or the observer moves, decide whether it rises or falls, and find the Mach number from the opening angle of the Mach cone.
Calculate acoustic impedances and the reflected fraction at boundaries, and apply the Doppler formula twice to a reflected wave, as in ultrasound imaging and Doppler sonography.
